name: Auca
confidence_why: Saint and Pike 1962 and Pike 1964, one body of first-hand fieldwork, describe Auca stress as set by the word's morphology (an alternating train from the first stem syllable and a second counted back from an unstressed final suffix syllable, several stresses per word), and the only other description, a single sentence in Peeke 1973 calling the default "normal penultimate stress" while deferring to Pike 1964 for phonology, matches the end of that suffix train rather than contradicting it, so the record rests on one detailed analysis with no dissent.

sweep_summary: Two title hits, both already listed and both about Waorani word stress. Pike 1964 'Stress trains in Auca' (the dedicated primary description that Saint & Pike 1962's footnote defers to) is held by the project in the open archive.org scan of the 1972 Brend reprint, pp.186-191; I read all six pages via the text and saved the extracted text. It confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding: a rightward stem train and a leftward suffix train (enclitics excluded) with clash/promotion rules at the stem-suffix junction yielding boundary-dependent phonemic contrasts; all stresses one phoneme, last optionally weakened. It should replace or join the 1962 summary as the deciding source (classification unchanged, 'rule' can now be filled from Rules 1A-1C, 2, 3A-3D). Lester 1994 (135-pp UTA MA thesis, UMI 1358869) remains unobtainable (ProQuest paywall; SIL/UTA/WorldCat blocked or absent; no open copy found); its Glottolog abstract restates the bidirectional root/suffix system and proposes a mono-directional metrical reanalysis, consistent with the classification; medium priority as a theoretical reanalysis rather than new data.org and direct site probes.

new_statements.quote: RULE 1A: A wave train starts from the end of words, with final suffixual syllable unstressed, alternating backwards to penultimate stress, antepenultimate nonstress, pro-antepenultimate stress, until the stem or fourth syllable is reached. [...] RULE 2: A second wave train starts from the beginning of the word - whether noun, verb, or attributive. When the stem is made up wholly of a single root, or of a sequence of roots without derivative suffixes, this stem train begins stressed and produces an alternating stress-nonstress syllable sequence (with a few special restrictions).

new_statements.reading: Stress placement is a function of morphological structure: an alternating train runs rightward from the first stem syllable (initial stressed) and a second train runs leftward from the last suffix syllable (final unstressed, penult stressed..), with enclitics outside the count and special clash/promotion rules where the two trains meet at the stem-suffix boundary (Rules 3B/3C), producing phonemic stress contrasts that depend only on where the boundary falls (apǽne.kándapa 'he speaks' vs dadó.ŋándapa 'he fished'). Pike treats all stresses as one phoneme with optional weakening of the last (Rule 4A), so no primary-stress edge is asserted. This is the catalog's 'morphological' classification, confirmed in full detail by the primary description.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement from Pike 1964 (Rule 1A: the end-anchored stress train leaves the final suffixal syllable unstressed and stresses the penult), so 'normal penultimate stress' is the surface summary of Pike's suffix train; Peeke adds a new detail, the emphatic stress-shift morpheme -V́ (final-vowel stress marks the Emphatic Sentence), which Pike's 1964 rules do not list (Pike's 'emphasis' is a separate enclitic /-taye/). Peeke says nothing about Pike's second, stem-initial train, the multiple stresses per word, or the boundary-conditioned contrasts, so her one-liner is a simplification, not a contradiction. new_statements.rule_in_words: Peeke gives no phonology chapter (the book is a tagmemic syntax of discourse, sentence and clause, and its introduction, pp. 3-4, refers the compiler to Pike 1964a and the Saint & Pike phonemics articles for the phonological analyses). Her only statement on word stress is incidental: normal stress is penultimate, and a suprasegmental emphasis morpheme -V́ (feature.05 'emphasis', creating the Emphatic Sentence type) moves the stress from the penult to the final vowel, e.g. go-kĩ-bo 'I shall go' -> gokibó 'shall I go?!'.
new_statements.exceptions: The emphatic morpheme -V́ shifts stress from the normal penult to the final vowel (pp. 20, 55). Paralinguistic/ideophonic speech may use 'extremes of pitch, stress, and length' outside the regular system (p. 14).
new_statements.identity_note: 'Auca' is the older exonym for Waorani/Huaorani (ISO 639-3 auc; PuRe record subject 'auc - Waorani'; Glottolog waor1240), an isolate of eastern Ecuador; Peeke (p. 3) identifies Ssabela with Auca and rejects the Zaparoan affiliation, and her data come from SIL fieldwork begun in 1958. No dialect is specified; the book is Peeke's 1968 Indiana PhD dissertation revised 1971.

readall_conflicts: No data conflict. Peeke 1973 describes the default as 'normal penultimate stress' in a single sentence (p. 55) without a phonology section, whereas the catalog's existing statement from Pike 1964 describes a two-train alternating system anchored at the word end (final suffix syllable unstressed, penult stressed) and at the stem start, with several stresses per word and boundary-conditioned contrasts. Pike's end-anchored train yields exactly the penultimate stress Peeke calls normal, so the two agree on the surface default; Peeke simply does not report the rest of the system (her introduction defers to Pike 1964a for phonology). One small terminological difference: Pike's 'emphasis' is the enclitic /-taye/ (which may itself carry stress), while Peeke's 'emphasis' marker.05 -V́ is a bare shift of stress to the final vowel; these are different morphemes, not competing analyses. The listed open copy (MPG PuRe item_400063, hdl 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-6B2D-2) is no longer open: its PDF component is visibility AUDIENCE (not reachable by automated download) behind an Anubis anti-bot page; the publisher's own SIL archive PDF (record 8858) is could not be reached by automated download but its 2024-06-26 Internet Archive copy served the file.

sources.note: The dedicated primary description of Waorani stress (whole 6-page paper is about it). Stress is computed over two morphologically defined domains: a suffix train counted from the word end (final suffix syllable unstressed, then alternating; enclitics excluded from the count, Rule 1C; five-suffix chains get Ca.CaCaCaCáCa, Rule 1B) and a stem train counted from the word beginning (initial stressed, alternating). sources.quote: The focus of this thesis is Waorani's stress system. It is viewed as the earliest recognized example of bi-directional stress: As one stress moves from left to right covering single roots and sequences of roots, a second stress moves from right to left covering suffixes. Waorani stress is interesting in that it exhibits two types of stress clash which are thought to be the result of the opposing stress waves. In view of the problems that exist with previous Waorani metrical analyses, I investigate the feasibility of a single stress wave (mono-directional) analysis which would have its epoch at the beginning of the word. (Glottolog abstract)
sources.note: The only monograph-length treatment of Waorani stress; abstract (Glottolog ref 121365) frames it as bidirectional root-vs-suffix stress with two clash types and tests a mono-directional alternative -- directly bears on whether 'morphological' or plain left-edge rhythmic (StressTyp's coding) is the right class, and may add data beyond Pike's.
